text: Version 3 is read as the current source even though its metadata table says Version 2, and version 4 is numbered from the file family; the Version 2 row of the superseded file is kept unchanged and not corrected in place.
why: An existing file is never edited and the next version is the highest version of the family plus 1, so the family number decides the new version and the metadata lag is recorded rather than resolved by editing the source.

text: The Wave 1 cutover is the first release named in version 3, 30 November 2026 (tentative), and the Wave 2, Wave 3 and Wave 4 release dates stay open with the placeholder of Template and Rules R9 until the release calendar states them.
why: The source names one release date only and Architecture v5 names no wave date, so the first release is the only date that can be attached to a wave without inventing one.
read: Version 3 section 1; Architecture v5 slide 38; Template and Rules U7, R9; AGENTS.md rule 10
confirm: Release owner with the programme governance group
impact: A wave cannot be scheduled and rehearsed until its date is stated; the Wave 1 rehearsal can start on this assumption.

text: One wave goes live per release, a release carries only the services of its own wave, and the cutover order inside a wave follows the connection matrix of Architecture v5 slide 13, with a service that others cache from first and the readers last.
why: The source releases one deployable a month and Architecture v5 gives waves without a release identifier, so one wave per release is the only mapping that keeps the monthly rhythm and the wave content of the architecture.
read: Version 3 section 2; Architecture v5 slides 13 and 38; Template and Rules R5.6
applied_in: Section 1; section 10.1; section 10.2 step 6; section 10.4; section 12 row 3
confirm: Release owner with the solution architect
impact: A wave that slips delays the waves after it; the order inside a wave can be changed without a new release if the matrix stays satisfied.

text: The first-release capabilities of version 3 are delivered by the nine Wave 1 services as read from the Architecture v5 contracts and the Ownership Map v1: case list in rwb-case, access in rwb-access, documents in rwb-document, notices in rwb-comms, ACE data in rwb-source-data, approvals and rules in rwb-decision, reporting in rwb-reporting, files in rwb-integration and agent runs in rwb-agent.
why: The source lists capabilities and the realignment needs a service per capability; the contracts of Architecture v5 name the owner of each one, so no capability is left unassigned and none is invented.
read: Version 3 section 7; Architecture v5 slides 14 to 20; Ownership Map v1 Services sheet
confirm: Solution architect with the nine Wave 1 service squads
impact: A capability that no Wave 1 service delivers would move to the wave of its service; the case list, access and documents are the three that must not move.

text: The rollback is per service: its flags off, its previous tag redeployed, in-flight cases kept on their recorded build through Worker Versioning, the previous rule package restored with one call, and the decision records kept locally and in the central ledger rather than rolled back.
why: With 19 services a wave-wide rollback would take live services down with the faulty one, and the Temporal and Drools design already gives the pinning and the one-call rule rollback that a per-service rollback needs.
read: Version 3 section 4; Architecture v5 slides 23 and 28; Temporal and Drools design T4 and the versioning section
applied_in: Section 4; section 10.3 Rollback gate; section 10.5; section 12 row 5
confirm: DevOps team with the platform team and the release owner
impact: A service can be reverted without stopping the wave; a fault that spans services still stops the wave and is handled by the release owner.

text: BOT approval under FPG 19/2560 clause 5.5 is treated as required before the Wave 1 cutover, with the submission date open, and it is carried as a gate in section 10.2 step 1 and as an open decision in section 9.
why: Architecture v5 names the dependency and says the date belongs in the plan; the source plan has no row for it, and leaving it out would let a wave start without a governance check that may take up to 30 business days.
read: Architecture v5 slides 6 and 38; version 3 section 9; AGENTS.md rule 9
applied_in: Section 1; section 9; section 10.2 step 1; section 10.5; section 12 row 6
impact: If the change is assessed as significant, Wave 1 cannot start until the approval is given; the platform work of Wave 0 is not affected.

why: Architecture v5 wins on source precedence and gives the views to one service with one login, and the check has to name the login that exists in the target design.

text: A wave is deployed into the existing ACE AKS cluster and namespace rwb-recovery, one api and one worker per service, with no new cluster capacity and no per-service slot count assumed; the capacity position is left open.
why: Architecture v5 places the 19 services in the shared ACE cluster and gives no production capacity figure, and the source deploys one tag, so any slot number would be invented.
